name: Online course business
blurb: Package a skill you know well into a video or cohort course and sell it online
title: Online Course Business: How to Create and Sell Online Courses
description: How an online course business makes money, what you need to sell online courses, who it suits, the hype to avoid and how to pre-sell before recording.
h1: How to start an online course business
answer: An online course business turns a skill you know well, from spreadsheets to sourdough, into lessons people pay for, either as self-paced videos or a live cohort. It earns one-off sales, subscriptions or memberships through a course platform, a marketplace or your own site. The catch is that making the course is the easy part; most of the work is finding buyers, and many courses sell very few copies.

sections.h: How an online course makes money
body: Self-paced courses sell once for a fixed price or as part of a membership. Live cohort courses charge more because they include your time, feedback and a group. Marketplaces bring traffic but set or discount prices and take a large share; your own site or a course platform keeps more of each sale but you must bring every buyer.
What eats the margin: platform and payment fees, refunds, advertising, support questions, and updating lessons when tools or rules change.

ul: Real, demonstrable skill in a topic, and ideally results you or others got from it.
A clear outcome: what a student can do after the course that they could not do before.
A microphone, screen recording or a camera, and simple editing software.
A course platform, marketplace or website with payments.
Honest marketing: avoid income or result promises you cannot back up. Advertising and consumer-protection rules apply to course sales in most countries.
A refund policy, terms of sale, sales-tax or VAT handling on digital products where required, and business registration as your country requires.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: Anyone selling a skill they have only just learned
People with an audience, mailing list or professional network
Those expecting the platform to bring buyers
Patient people who like improving lessons from feedback
People wanting to record once and never update

ul: No audience: without a way to reach buyers, a finished course can sit unsold.

The "course about making courses" trap: many coaching programmes earn from aspiring creators. The US Federal Trade Commission lists guaranteed income, invented success stories and pressure to pay quickly as signs of a coaching scam.
Marketplace dependence: price discounts and rule changes on large platforms are out of your control.
Refunds and piracy: some buyers watch and refund, and videos get shared. Keep the price fair and add live or community value that cannot be copied.
Outdated content in fast-moving topics such as software or social media.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Teach the topic for free once, in a short workshop, video or post, and watch which questions come up.
Write an outline and a one-page sales description with a price.
Pre-sell to your network or audience before recording, with a full refund if you do not run it.
Run the first version live to a small group and record it.
Turn the questions and feedback into the self-paced version only if students got results.
Choose one narrow outcome and one type of student.
Outline short lessons, each with a task the student completes.
Set up the platform, checkout, refund policy and a welcome email.
Run or record the first cohort and collect feedback after each lesson.
Gather honest testimonials and fix the weakest lessons.
Plan one steady channel for finding students, such as a newsletter, videos or partnerships.

faq.q: Should I sell on a course marketplace or my own site?
faq.a: A marketplace can bring buyers when you have no audience, but it controls pricing and keeps more of each sale. Your own site or a course platform keeps more revenue and your customer list, but you must market it yourself. Some creators use both.

faq.q: Do I need to be certified to sell an online course?
faq.a: Usually not for general skills. Topics such as finance, health or law can carry legal limits on what you may advise or promise, so check the rules where you and your students are.

faq.q: How long should an online course be?
faq.a: As short as it can be while still delivering the promised outcome. Students value finishing and getting results more than hours of video.
